title: Windows
description: Windows cinematography treats panes as the true subject: stacked apertures, lives in rectangles, a building of frames. The diagram is a grid of possible pictures, not one doorway around one face.

sections.title: Narrative function

blocks.text: A facade at night is a contact sheet of other people's rooms. A courtyard is a theater of windows.
Who owns space changes per rectangle: a cook, a sleeper, a fighter, an empty kitchen. The building is a montage that does not cut.
It is the wrong tool when you only need one inner frame around one encounter. That is a single frame-within-frame.
If the other panes do no work, you photographed a house. Windows can be looked through from inside (rain on glass, a face and a street) or looked at from outside (Rear Window grammar).
Decide which side of the glass we occupy, and whether reflections will stack a second world.

sections.title: How it works

blocks.text: Find a true grid: a courtyard, a block of apartments, an office elevation. Use a longer lens to flatten panes into a sheet of rectangles, or a wider lens if we are inside one room looking at many across a court.

Expose so more than one interior reads, or so most go dark except the one that matters. Prompt: Windows as the true subject around [Subject], stacked apertures, lives in rectangles, a building of frames.

sections.title: When to use it

blocks.text: Use it when many lives share a building, or when a single life is one pane among others. Do not use it as a pretty rain window on a portrait that never acknowledges other rooms.

sections.title: Compared with similar shots

blocks.text: Frame within Frame is usually one inner rectangle. Windows multiplies them.
Screen in Screen nests electronic pictures. These are architectural pictures.
Voyeur may watch one pane from concealment. Windows can also be a public elevation, a city showing itself.
Repetition and Pattern counts the grid. Here the content of each cell matters.
Reflections may write the street onto the same glass.

sections.title: In film

blocks.text: Rear Window turns a courtyard of windows into a set of simultaneous shorts. The Hours uses windows as thresholds between interior lives and the weather of a city.
A building becomes an editing machine you can hold. Grammar of panes, not a single pretty rain glass.

sections.title: Prompt it

blocks.text: Make the panes the subject. Windows as the true subject around [Subject], stacked apertures, lives in rectangles, a building of frames.
Say courtyard facade at night, multiple lit interiors, or a wall of office panes. Place the subject in one rectangle among others.
Name at least two other lives or empty rooms.

sections.title: What usually goes wrong

blocks.text: The usual wrong cousin is a single rain-streaked portrait, or a Frame within Frame doorway. The tell is one face and one glass with no other cells.
The fix is to show a grid of apertures and to give at least one other pane a life, even if it is only a lamp and an empty chair.

sections.title: Questions

blocks.text: What is windows in film?
Panes become the subject: stacked apertures, lives in rectangles, a building of frames. The composition is a grid of possible shots. One person may occupy one cell. The other cells still work.
Windows vs Frame within Frame

Frame within a frame is typically one inner border around the action, a door or arch. Windows multiplies apertures until the building is a sheet of pictures. A single window around a couple is doorway grammar. A courtyard of ten lit rooms is windows.
When should I use windows?
Use it when many lives share glass: apartments, offices, a courtyard at night, a city block. Skip it when you only need one threshold around one encounter.
How do I prompt windows for AI image or video?

Ask for stacked panes and multiple lives. Example: Windows as the true subject around [Subject], stacked apertures, lives in rectangles, a building of frames. Specify a facade or courtyard and more than one lit interior. Place the subject in one cell.
